cfg.last_pass_note: The Biochemistry questions taken from cases asked in class, slide exercises and facts flagged on slides with NOTE, N.B. or REMEMBER.

items.q: A client with high LDL-cholesterol asks how much treatment can lower it. The nurse explains that diet control lowers total and LDL-cholesterol by about {1}, while a statin lowers them by about {2}.
items.w: Total blood cholesterol varies with diet and endogenous synthesis. Treating hypercholesterolemia by diet control or by drugs lowers LDL-cholesterol, raises HDL-cholesterol and reduces CHD risk. Diet control alone gives a 10-20% reduction in total and LDL-cholesterol; hypocholesterolemic drugs such as statins give 30-40%. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.0:2: 1-2% is not the figure given; diet control gives 10-20%.
x.1:1: 10-20% is the reduction with diet control.
x.1:2: 60-70% is not the figure given; statins give 30-40%.

items.q: A client asks which foods are main sources of saturated fat. Which foods should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
items.w: Saturated fats are triacylglycerols whose fatty acids have no double bonds. Their main sources are dairy and meat products and some vegetable oils, notably coconut and palm oils. Saturated fat intake is strongly associated with high total and LDL-cholesterol and high CHD risk, so intake should be limited. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.4: Olive oil is mainly monounsaturated (oleic acid).
x.5: Corn oil is an omega-6 polyunsaturated fat.
x.6: Flaxseed oil is a plant source of omega-3 alpha-linolenic acid.

m.4: thinks all oils are unsaturated or all are saturated

items.q: A client replaces butter with olive oil in cooking. Which change in blood lipids should the nurse expect?
o: Lower total and LDL-cholesterol with higher HDL-cholesterol
Lower total and LDL-cholesterol with lower HDL-cholesterol
Lower triacylglycerol with little effect on LDL or HDL
items.w: Olive oil is rich in monounsaturated fat (oleic acid, one double bond). Substituting monounsaturated for saturated fatty acids lowers total and LDL-cholesterol and increases HDL-cholesterol, lowering CHD risk. Mediterranean diets rich in olive oil show a low incidence of CHD. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.1: Lowering HDL too is the pattern of omega-6 fats.
x.2: This is the pattern of trans fats.
x.3: This is the pattern of omega-3 fats.

m.1: mixes up MUFA and omega-6 effects
m.2: mixes up MUFA and trans fat effects
m.3: mixes up MUFA and omega-3 effects

items.q: A client uses large amounts of corn and sunflower oil to protect the heart. Which effect of these oils limits their benefit?
o: They lower HDL-cholesterol as well and have a proinflammatory effect.
They are not essential fatty acids.
items.w: Corn, sesame, cottonseed and sunflower oils are rich in omega-6 polyunsaturated fat such as linoleic acid (18:2 n-6), an essential fatty acid needed for membrane fluidity and eicosanoid synthesis. They lower total and LDL-cholesterol, but they also lower HDL-cholesterol and are proinflammatory, which decreases their effect on CHD. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.1: Omega-6 oils LOWER total and LDL-cholesterol; raising LDL is a trans fat effect.
x.2: Dietary cholesterol is found only in animal products.
x.3: Linoleic acid, the omega-6 in these oils, IS an essential fatty acid.

items.q: A client with high triglycerides asks about eating fatty fish such as salmon and sardines. Which effects of omega-3 fats should the nurse describe? Select all that apply.
o: Decreasing the tendency to vascular thrombosis
items.w: Omega-3 fats come from plants (alpha-linolenic acid in flaxseed and walnuts) and fatty fish (EPA and DHA in salmon, mackerel, anchovies, sardines, herring and tuna). They reduce CHD risk by suppressing arrhythmia, reducing blood triacylglycerol, decreasing thrombosis and reducing inflammation, with little effect on LDL- and HDL-cholesterol. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.4: Omega-3 fats have LITTLE effect on LDL- and HDL-cholesterol.
x.5: Lowering HDL is an omega-6 effect.

m.5: mixes up omega-3 and omega-6 effects

items.q: A nurse explains fatty acid naming to a client. In an omega-3 fat, the first double bond begins at carbon number ____ counting from the methyl end.
items.w: The omega number is the position of the first double bond counted from the methyl end of the fatty acid. Omega-3 fats begin at the 3rd carbon, omega-6 fats (linoleic acid) at the 6th and the monounsaturated oleic acid is omega-9. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.1: Carbon 6 marks omega-6 fats such as linoleic acid.
x.2: Carbon 9 marks omega-9 fats such as oleic acid (monounsaturated).

items.q: A vegetarian client wants an essential omega-3 fatty acid from plant foods. Which fatty acid should the nurse identify?
o: Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) from flaxseed oil and walnuts
items.w: Plant sources (flaxseed oils, walnuts) provide alpha-linolenic acid, an essential omega-3 fatty acid needed at 0.6-1.2% of total calories, with double bonds at carbons 9, 12 and 15. Fatty fish provide EPA (20 carbons, 5 double bonds) and DHA (22 carbons, 6 double bonds), which are not essential. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.1: EPA comes from fatty fish oils and is not an essential fatty acid.
x.2: DHA (22 carbons, 6 double bonds) comes from fatty fish oils, not walnuts.
x.3: Oleic acid is a monounsaturated omega-9 fat.

m.1: thinks EPA is a plant essential fatty acid

items.q: A nurse teaches a client how to spot trans fats when shopping. Which words on an ingredient list indicate trans fatty acids?
items.w: Trans fatty acids are not found in plants and occur only in small amounts in animal foods, but they are formed during hydrogenation of liquid vegetable oils, as in margarine manufacture. The key to their presence in a food is the words "partially hydrogenated" on the ingredient list. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD), slide note (key to trans fats))

x.1: Olive oil is a monounsaturated fat, not a trans fat.
x.2: Plant sterols lower LDL by blocking cholesterol absorption.

m.2: confuses plant sterols with trans fats

items.q: A nurse explains that trans fatty acids are chemically unsaturated but behave more like saturated fatty acids.
items.w: True. Trans fatty acids are chemically classified as unsaturated, but they behave more like saturated fatty acids: they raise LDL-cholesterol, lower HDL-cholesterol and increase CHD risk. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.1: This statement is true: trans fats are unsaturated yet act like saturated fats.

items.q: A nurse states that WHO recommends limiting trans fat to less than 10% of total energy intake.
items.w: False. WHO recommends limiting trans fat to less than 1% of total energy intake, which is less than 2.2 g per day on a 2000-calorie diet. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.0: The WHO limit is less than 1% of energy (under 2.2 g/day on 2000 kcal).

items.q: A nurse reviews dietary fats with a client. Match each type of fat to its effect on blood lipids.

choices: Lowers triacylglycerol with little effect on LDL or HDL

items.w: Each fat has a signature effect. Saturated fats raise total and LDL-cholesterol. Trans fats raise LDL and lower HDL. Monounsaturated fats lower LDL and raise HDL. Omega-6 fats lower both LDL and HDL. Omega-3 fats lower triacylglycerol, suppress arrhythmia, thrombosis and inflammation, with little effect on LDL or HDL. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.4: Lowering both LDL and HDL is the effect of omega-6 fats.

m.4: mixes up omega-3 and omega-6 effects

rs.0: A client eats a diet high in saturated fat. Which effect on blood lipids should the nurse expect?
rs.1: A client eats many foods made with partially hydrogenated oil. Which lipid effect should the nurse expect?
rs.2: A client substitutes monounsaturated fat for saturated fat. Which lipid effect should the nurse expect?
rs.3: A client adds fish oil (omega-3) to the diet. Which lipid effect should the nurse expect?

items.q: A nurse teaches a client about diet and cholesterol. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
o: "The cholesterol I eat affects my blood cholesterol more than the type of fat I eat."
"Cholesterol is found only in animal products."
"Plant sterols lower LDL by blocking cholesterol absorption in my gut."
items.w: Dietary cholesterol is found only in animal products, but its effect on blood cholesterol is LESS important than the amount and type of fatty acids eaten. A client who believes the opposite needs more teaching. Plant sterols in fortified margarines reduce LDL by blocking cholesterol absorption, and fish oils reduce triacylglycerol. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.1: This is accurate: dietary cholesterol is found only in animal products, so no teaching is needed.
x.2: This is accurate: plant sterols inhibit intestinal absorption of cholesterol.
x.3: This is accurate: omega-3 fish oils reduce blood triacylglycerol.

items.q: A client with high cholesterol asks which dietary factors help lower blood cholesterol. Which factors should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Antioxidants such as vitamins E and C
items.w: The dietary factors listed as decreasing blood cholesterol are omega-6 polyunsaturated fats, monounsaturated fats, antioxidants (beta carotene, vitamins E and C), plant sterols, vegetable fiber and large doses of vitamin B3. Saturated and trans fats push cholesterol the other way. (Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD))

x.5: Saturated fats RAISE total and LDL-cholesterol.
x.6: Partially hydrogenated oils contain trans fats, which raise LDL.

m.6: thinks margarine trans fats are protective

items.q: A nurse explains oxidative stress to a client with coronary disease. Which definition is accurate?
o: An imbalance favoring oxidants and/or disfavoring antioxidants that can lead to damage
Any production of reactive oxygen species in the body
An excess of antioxidants over oxidants
The buildup of lipid-rich plaque in the intima
items.w: Oxidative stress is a state in which reactive species increase without a matching increase in antioxidants: an imbalance favoring oxidants and/or disfavoring antioxidants, potentially leading to damage. Reactive oxygen species are not always harmful; phagocytes use them to kill microbes. The imbalance is what has been implicated in diseases such as atherosclerosis. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.1: ROS are made normally and can be useful (e.g. microbial killing); stress is the IMBALANCE.
x.2: That is the opposite of oxidative stress.
x.3: That describes atherosclerosis, which oxidative stress helps cause.

m.1: thinks any ROS is oxidative stress

items.q: A nurse reviews reactive nitrogen species. Which one is a NON-radical?
items.w: Reactive species are split into radicals, which carry an unpaired electron, and non-radicals, which are strong oxidants or favor strong oxidant formation. Among reactive nitrogen species, nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide are radicals and peroxynitrite is a non-radical. Among reactive oxygen species, superoxide, hydroxyl and peroxyl are radicals; hydrogen peroxide, hypochlorous acid and ozone are not. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.1: Nitric oxide (NO.) is a free radical.
x.2: Nitrogen dioxide (NO2.) is a free radical.
x.3: Superoxide is a reactive OXYGEN species and a radical.

items.q: A nurse states that hydrogen peroxide is a free radical because it has an unpaired electron.
items.w: False. Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is a NON-radical reactive oxygen species: a strong oxidant without an unpaired electron. The ROS radicals are superoxide, hydroxyl and peroxyl. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

items.q: A nurse reviews ENDOGENOUS sources of free radicals in a client's cells. Which sources apply? Select all that apply.
o: Leakage of electrons from the respiratory chain
items.w: Endogenous free radicals come from cellular metabolism: electron leakage from the respiratory chain, oxidase enzymes such as xanthine oxidase, prostaglandin synthesis, production of nitric oxide from arginine and phagocytosis (myeloperoxidase, NADPH oxidase). Exogenous sources are drug metabolism, ionizing radiation and cigarette smoke. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.4: Cigarette smoke is an exogenous (environmental) source.
x.5: Ionizing radiation is an exogenous source.
x.6: Drug metabolism (halothane, cytochrome P450) is listed as exogenous.

m.4: mixes up endogenous and exogenous sources
m.5: mixes up endogenous and exogenous sources

items.q: A client's neutrophils engulf bacteria. Arrange the steps of the oxygen-dependent killing pathway in order.
o: Bacteria are phagocytosed and ROS production rises (respiratory burst)
NADPH oxidase converts molecular oxygen into superoxide
Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide into hydrogen peroxide
Myeloperoxidase converts H2O2 and chloride into hypochlorous acid
items.w: Reactive oxygen species are sometimes useful. In neutrophils and monocytes, phagocytosis triggers a rapid rise in ROS called the respiratory burst. NADPH oxidase converts oxygen to superoxide, superoxide dismutase converts it to H2O2, and myeloperoxidase uses H2O2 and chloride ions to make hypochlorous acid, which kills bacteria. H2O2 can also form hydroxyl radicals in a reaction catalyzed by free ferrous ions. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

items.q: A client with severe sepsis has very high nitric oxide production driven by bacterial toxins and cytokines. Which enzyme is responsible?
items.w: Nitric oxide is made from L-arginine by NO synthase. eNOS (endothelium) and nNOS (neural) are constitutive and produce low levels constantly. iNOS is expressed in many cells including macrophages and neutrophils; it is induced by bacterial toxins, TNF and inflammatory cytokines and can produce large amounts of NO for hours or days, so it is linked to inflammation. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.1: eNOS is constitutive and constantly produces LOW levels of NO.
x.2: nNOS is constitutive and produces low levels of NO in neurons.
x.3: Xanthine oxidase is an oxidase that produces ROS, not NO.

items.q: A client with angina takes sublingual nitroglycerin. How does it relieve coronary spasm?
o: It is metabolized into nitric oxide, which causes vasodilation.
It is converted into superoxide, which relaxes smooth muscle.
It acts as an antioxidant that neutralizes oxidized LDL.
items.w: NO produced by endothelial NOS improves vascular dilation and perfusion, which is beneficial. Vasodilators such as nitroglycerin are metabolized into NO and so dilate coronary arteries in spasm in angina, a therapeutic and diagnostic use. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.1: Superoxide is a damaging ROS radical, not a vasodilator.
x.2: Nitroglycerin works through NO-mediated vasodilation, not as an antioxidant.
x.3: iNOS induction is linked to inflammation, not to nitroglycerin's therapeutic effect.

m.3: mixes up iNOS and therapeutic NO

items.q: A nurse explains that nitric oxide is a free-radical gas with a half-life of seconds that is made from L-arginine.
items.w: True. NO is a free radical gas with a very short half-life (seconds), synthesized by NO synthase from L-arginine and metabolized into nitrates, nitrites and peroxynitrite. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.1: This statement is true: NO is a short-lived radical made from L-arginine.

items.q: A nurse reviews the body's antioxidant defenses with a client. Match each antioxidant to its type.
items.w: Antioxidants are enzymatic (superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase with glutathione reductase and G6PD) or non-enzymatic. Non-enzymatic antioxidants are nutrient (carotene, tocopherol, ascorbic acid, selenium) or metabolic (glutathione, thioredoxin, ceruloplasmin, albumin, melatonin, transferrin, ferritin, uric acid). (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.3: Transition metals favor the formation of strong oxidants; they are not antioxidants.

rs.0: A nurse explains how superoxide dismutase protects cells. What type of antioxidant is it?
rs.1: A client takes vitamin E supplements. What type of antioxidant is vitamin E?
rs.2: A nurse describes glutathione to a client. What type of antioxidant is it?
rs.3: A nurse reviews catalase. What type of antioxidant is it?

items.q: A nurse explains how oxidized LDL drives atherosclerosis. Arrange the key stages in order.
o: Endothelial dysfunction from hypertension, smoking or dyslipidemia
LDL enters the intima and is oxidized
Adhesion molecules (VCAM-1, ICAM-1) and MCP-1 recruit monocytes
Macrophages engulf oxidized LDL and become foam cells (fatty streak)
Smooth muscle cells migrate and form a fibrous cap
Plaque rupture or erosion triggers thrombosis
items.w: Stressors damage the endothelium. LDL passes into the intima and is oxidized by free radicals and lipoxygenases. Activated endothelium expresses VCAM-1, ICAM-1 and MCP-1 that recruit monocytes and T cells. Monocytes become macrophages that engulf oxidized LDL via scavenger receptors and become foam cells, forming the fatty streak. Smooth muscle cells migrate from the media, proliferate and lay down a fibrous cap; a necrotic core and calcification follow, and a vulnerable plaque may rupture and trigger thrombosis. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress), key stages slide)

items.q: A nurse explains how fatty streaks form in a client's arteries. How do macrophages take up oxidized LDL?
o: Through scavenger receptors, turning into lipid-laden foam cells
Through VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 on the macrophage
By efferocytosis of dead smooth muscle cells
By secreting collagen around the lipid
items.w: Monocytes recruited into the intima differentiate into macrophages and engulf oxidized LDL via scavenger receptors, becoming lipid-laden foam cells. The initial accumulation of foam cells creates the earliest visible lesion, the fatty streak. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.1: VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 are adhesion molecules on activated ENDOTHELIAL cells that capture monocytes.
x.2: Efferocytosis is clearing dead cells; its failure enlarges the necrotic core.
x.3: Collagen and proteoglycans are made by smooth muscle cells forming the fibrous cap.

m.1: mixes up adhesion molecules and scavenger receptors

items.q: A nurse reviews why some atherosclerotic plaques develop a large necrotic core. Which process is responsible?
o: Apoptosis of macrophages and SMCs with impaired clearance of the dead cells (efferocytosis)
Migration of smooth muscle cells to form a fibrous cap
Expression of VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 by endothelial cells
items.w: As plaques progress, macrophages and smooth muscle cells undergo apoptosis and secondary necrosis. When the dead cells are not cleared (impaired efferocytosis), an acellular necrotic core rich in lipids and debris enlarges, and calcium salts deposit, causing calcification. Vulnerable plaques can then rupture or erode and trigger thrombosis. (Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress))

x.1: SMC migration builds the fibrous cap over the lipid core, not the necrotic core.
x.2: Adhesion molecules recruit monocytes early in the process.
x.3: Blocking intestinal cholesterol absorption is how plant sterols lower LDL.

m.1: mixes up cap formation and necrotic core

bio-lipids-chd.title: Blood lipids and coronary heart disease
points: Total blood cholesterol comes from diet and endogenous synthesis and is carried by lipoproteins, especially LDL and HDL.
CHD risk rises with total and LDL cholesterol; high HDL-cholesterol is associated with decreased risk.
Diet control lowers TC and LDL-C by 10-20%; statins lower them by 30-40%.

bio-fats.title: Types of dietary fat and their effects
points: Saturated fats (no double bonds; dairy, meat, coconut and palm oils) raise TC and LDL-C and CHD risk.
Monounsaturated fats (one double bond; olive oil, oleic acid, omega-9) lower TC and LDL-C and raise HDL-C when substituted for saturated fats.
Omega-6 fats (first double bond at carbon 6 from the methyl end; corn, sesame, cottonseed, sunflower oils) lower TC and LDL-C but also lower HDL-C and are proinflammatory.
Omega-3 fats suppress arrhythmia, reduce blood triacylglycerol, decrease thrombosis and inflammation, with little effect on LDL-C and HDL-C.
Trans fats are chemically unsaturated but behave like saturated fats: they raise LDL-C and lower HDL-C; formed by partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils (margarine).
bio-fats.source: Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD)

bio-cholesterol-sterols.title: Dietary cholesterol, plant sterols and cholesterol-lowering factors
points: Dietary cholesterol is found only in animal products; its effect on blood cholesterol is less important than the amount and type of fatty acids.
Plant sterols reduce LDL-cholesterol by inhibiting intestinal absorption of cholesterol.
Dietary factors that decrease blood cholesterol: omega-6 PUFA, MUFA, antioxidants (beta carotene, vitamins E and C), plant sterols, vegetable fiber, large-dose vitamin B3.

bio-ros.title: Free radicals, ROS and RNS
points: Oxidative stress: an imbalance favoring oxidants and/or disfavoring antioxidants, potentially leading to damage.
A free radical is a molecule with an unpaired electron in an outer valence shell; it plucks an electron from the nearest molecule.
ROS radicals: superoxide, hydroxyl, peroxyl. ROS non-radicals: hydrogen peroxide, hypochlorous acid, ozone.
RNS radicals: nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide. RNS non-radical: peroxynitrite.

Endogenous sources: electron leak from the respiratory chain, oxidases (xanthine oxidase), prostaglandin synthesis, NO from arginine, phagocytosis. Exogenous: drug metabolism (halothane, cytochrome P450), ionizing radiation, cigarette smoke.

bio-oxldl.title: Oxidized LDL and the stages of atherosclerosis
points: Free radicals oxidize LDL cholesterol; oxidized LDL triggers inflammation and plaque buildup.

Stages: endothelial dysfunction, LDL retention and oxidation in the intima, recruitment of monocytes and T cells by VCAM-1, ICAM-1 and MCP-1, foam cell formation (fatty streak), SMC migration and fibrous cap, necrotic core and calcification, rupture or erosion with thrombosis.
Macrophages engulf oxidized LDL via scavenger receptors and become lipid-laden foam cells.
Failure to clear dead macrophages and SMCs (impaired efferocytosis) enlarges an acellular necrotic core.
